A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same risk-controlled early-exit framework, despite the changed title and expanded scope. The main text, figures, equations and complete appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original risk-control, efficiency and ablation experiments across eight classification tasks and four models.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original SQuAD v2.0 question-answering results and fallback analyses using T5-Large/CALM.

M1.justification: The confidence-based early exit, zero-shot baseline, relative loss and risk transformation remain intact. v2 adds a multi-token inference adaptation: token-wise exits with answer-level zero-shot fallback when every generated token fails to exceed the confidence threshold at every layer (Appendices B.2 and J.5).

E1.justification: v2 adds SQuAD v2.0 open-ended, multi-token question answering with helpful and misleading context to the eight retained classification tasks. This substantially extends task requirements beyond finite-label in-context learning (Section 4.2).

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison remains risk transformation versus negative-loss clipping, with existing full-model and zero-shot comparisons retained. v2 extends that comparison to QA; CALM/T5 supplies the new experimental model rather than an additional separately reported comparator (Figures 8, 16 and 17).

E3.justification: The new QA protocol uses T5-Large/CALM, question-only full-model zero-shot predictions, 50/50 helpful/harmful calibration, and up to five GPT-5-generated reference answers for unanswerable questions (Appendix B.2). The existing ICL splits, label transformations, contextual calibration and first-exit settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds QA context-mixture analyses, a diagnostic of fallback frequency and benefit, and an ablation comparing all-token, any-token and average-confidence fallback rules (Section 4.3; Appendices G and J.5). These provide substantive new evidence about sequence-level fallback behavior; the original ICL analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report one-standard-error bands over 100 experiments and bootstrap confidence intervals in Appendix F. v2 extends the existing reporting practice to QA without stating changes to repetition counts, seeds or statistical estimation procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds QA risk and efficiency curves and reports fallback on 3.0% of unanswerable versus 0.9% of answerable questions, with zero-shot outperforming early exit on 71% of unanswerable fallback cases (Section 4.3). Appendix J.5 adds fallback-rate results. The main ICL risk/efficiency curves are retained, while Figure 4's histogram proportions change slightly.

T1.justification: Section 2 broadens the formal answer space from finite classification labels to potentially unbounded answers and distinguishes general context from ICL demonstrations. The relative-loss construction, affine risk transformation and Appendix C proof remain mathematically unchanged; Equation 2 is shortened equivalently.

C1.justification: v1's central claims concern safe in-context learning from demonstrations. v2 broadens them to controlling harmful user-provided context across classification and open-ended QA, explicitly claiming coverage of nine tasks and five models. This expanded applicability appears in the title, abstract, introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the QA fallback statistics as evidence of selective intervention on harmful context and adds a rationale for choosing the all-token fallback rule. The limitation that marginal risk guarantees do not ensure subgroup guarantees remains, with its detailed discussion moved to Appendix H.

D1.justification: Appendices B.2 and J.5 add QA reference-generation and fallback implementation details. Hardware and ICL prompt disclosures remain. However, v2 removes v1's reproducibility statement and experiment source-code link; the PDFs do not establish any change in the repository's actual availability.

R1.justification: v2 adds the T5 and SQuAD references by Raffel et al. and Rajpurkar et al., while removing the attack references by Anil et al., Das et al. and Liu et al. The main positioning against prior risk-control and early-exit work remains, with broader context-oriented framing.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, rewrites the abstract and introductory motivation, and extensively replaces demonstration-specific language with general-context terminology. Experiments are reorganized around ICL and QA; existing experimental-design details move to Appendix B and detailed subgroup discussion to Appendix H.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, extensively resizes and redistributes existing figures, and adds QA Figures 6, 8, 16 and 17. Figure 3's axis labels and Figure 4's titles change. The new Figures 16 and 17 show different curves but carry identical context-mixture descriptions, creating a labeling ambiguity.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens empirical support beyond classification through QA experiments and tests of alternative sequence-fallback rules, while retaining v1's theory and main results. The net benefit is limited by missing validation details for GPT-5-generated reference answers, ambiguous mixture captions in Figures 16–17, and omission of v1's code link.
